y0: Why start with a family tree?
y1: In the first sentence, Matthew introduces Jesus as the Messiah, the 'Son of David' and the son of Abraham. For the first readers, the Jews, a family tree was like an ID card. Because the promised Messiah absolutely had to come from David's line.
y2: God had told Abraham, 'In you all the families of the earth will be blessed', and to David, 'Your throne will be established forever'. Matthew shows that Jesus is the owner of these two promises.
y3: Hebrew letters were also used as numbers. The name David (דוד) adds up to ד(4)+ו(6)+ד(4)=14. Many scholars think that Matthew emphasizes the idea of the 'Son of David' by dividing the family tree into three parts of 14 generations.
y5: At that time, a Jewish engagement was a more serious promise than it is today. According to the law, they were already considered husband and wife, and breaking the engagement required a divorce. Usually, about a year later, the groom would take the bride to his home, and they would start living together.
y6: During this time, Mary becomes pregnant through the Holy Spirit. Matthew clearly shows that this is not a human plan, but a work done by God Himself.
y7: The choice of Joseph, a righteous man
y8: According to the law, Joseph could have brought this matter up in front of everyone. But he does not want to disgrace Mary and decides to leave secretly. The righteousness Matthew talks about is combining obedience to the law with loving a person.
y9: Then an angel says to him in a dream, 'Joseph, son of David, don't be afraid,' and instructs him to name the baby Jesus. Because He will save His people from their sins.
y10: The name 'Jesus' comes from the Hebrew name 'Yeshua' and means 'The Lord saves.' Many Jews were waiting for a Messiah who would free them from Roman rule. But the angel says that what Jesus will save them from is 'sin.' This means He came to solve a much deeper problem.
y11: “So that the promise would be fulfilled”
y12: Matthew says that this event happened to fulfill the word of the prophet Isaiah. In the Gospel of Matthew, this kind of 'fulfillment' expression appears more than ten times. Matthew wants to show that Jesus' whole life is the completion of the promises in the Old Testament.
y13: That child's name is Immanuel, which means 'God is with us.'
y14: The Gospel of Matthew begins in 1:23 with the words 'God is with us' and ends in 28:20 with Jesus' promise, 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age.' The whole book is surrounded by the theme of 'God with us.'
y16: Joseph wakes up from his sleep and takes Mary to his home as the angel commanded. When the baby is born, he names him Jesus.
y17: Not a single word spoken by Joseph is recorded in the Bible. His faith is shown by actions, not words. A father naming a child meant legally accepting that child as his own son. Because of this, Jesus becomes the 'Son of David' through Joseph.
verse: “She will bring forth a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for it is he who will save his people from their sins.”
prayer: Lord God, we thank You for not forgetting Your promise from long ago and sending Jesus. We learned about Your grace that embraces even people with mistakes and wounds. Help us to believe and obey Your word even when we don't understand, just like Joseph did. We pray in the name of Immanuel, Jesus Christ. Amen.
d0: family tree. A record writing a family's lineage from generation to generation. In Jewish society, it was an important document proving which tribe and which family someone belonged to. The word 'genesis' in Matthew 1:1 is the same as the name of the book of Genesis. This gives the feeling of the beginning of a new creation.
d1: Messiah. It means 'Anointed one.' In the Old Testament, oil was poured on the head when a king or priest was appointed. This word refers to the Savior King promised by God. 'Jesus Christ' is not a first and last name, but an expression of faith that 'Jesus is the Christ.'
d2: Son of David. Because God promised David an eternal throne, the Jews called the Messiah the 'Son of David.' In the Gospel of Matthew, sick people cry out several times, 'Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!'
d3: engagement. At that time, engagement was legally the same as being husband and wife. Even though engaged couples did not live together, a divorce paper was needed to break the engagement. In verses 19–20, Joseph is called Mary's 'husband' and Mary is called Joseph's 'wife.'
d4: the Holy Spirit. God's Spirit. The Spirit of God, who moved when the world was created in Genesis 1, is now making a new beginning. Jesus being conceived in the womb was not by human power, but by God's power.
d5: righteous. Living according to God's will. In the Gospel of Matthew, righteousness is not just following rules, but it goes together with mercy. It is connected to Jesus' words, 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice' (Matt. 9:13).
d6: Jesus. It is the same as the name Joshua in the Old Testament. It means 'The Lord saves'; the name itself indicates Jesus' mission. Just as Joshua led the people to the promised land, Jesus leads the people to salvation from sin.
d7: sin. It actually means 'failing to hit the target.' It refers to the state and actions that have strayed from the purpose for which God created us. Sin is not just a few bad deeds, but the heart turning away from God.
d8: save. It also carries the meanings of rescuing from danger, healing sickness, and making a person whole. In the Gospel of Matthew, the same word is also used for the 'healing' of the sick.
d9: prophet. A person who receives God's word and delivers it to the people. They also spoke about the future, but mostly they called the people to return to God. Isaiah lived about 700 years before Jesus.
d10: fulfill. It means to complete a promise, like filling an empty vessel. It is one of the main words in the Gospel of Matthew. This word is also in the verse, 'I didn't come to destroy the law or the prophets, but to fulfill' (Matt. 5:17).
d11: Immanuel. 'Immanu' means 'with us', and 'El' means 'God'. It means that God is not far away, but a God who comes among us. It forms a pair with the final promise in Matthew 28:20.
